title: The Sun Stands Still
lead: At the battle of Gibeon Joshua commanded the sun and moon to stand still, quoting the Book of Jashar, and "there has never been a day like that one" (Joshua 10:12–14). The passage has been read as a cosmic miracle, a darkening, an omen, or battle poetry.

sections.h: The long day in the Bible and after
sections.b: The only account is Joshua 10:12–14. Habakkuk 3:11 recalls it in a hymn of God's warfare: "Sun and moon stand still in their lofty home." Sirach 46:4 praises Joshua: "Was it not by his hand that the sun stepped back, and a single day stretched to two?" Isaiah 38:8 tells of a different sign, the shadow going back on Ahaz's stairway for Hezekiah. The verse became famous in the 16th and 17th centuries when it was cited against Copernicus and Galileo. Modern readers divide over whether it describes a literal halt, a prolonged light, an eclipse or darkening, an omen, or poetic language like "the stars fought from heaven" (Judges 5:20).
